claims.text: Rapidly quenched HfNbTaTiZr has minimal local atomic disorder and provides a low-disorder baseline.
Controlled annealing of HfNbTaTiZr increases local atomic disorder relative to rapid quenching.
Diffraction lattice-parameter shifts and peak broadening can quantify the degree of local atomic disorder in this alloy.
Thermal activation increases atomic displacements and thereby enhances local lattice disorder.
Greater local atomic disorder produces heterogeneous lattice distortions.
Disorder-induced lattice distortions lower effective elastic bond strength and elastic moduli.
Local disorder alters dislocation nucleation barriers.
Annealed, higher-disorder HfNbTaTiZr will have a lower elastic modulus than the rapidly quenched baseline.
Annealed, higher-disorder HfNbTaTiZr will have a lower yield strength than the rapidly quenched baseline.
Annealed, higher-disorder HfNbTaTiZr will have a higher thermal-expansion coefficient than the rapidly quenched baseline.
The changes in modulus, yield strength, and thermal-expansion coefficient will scale with the degree of atomic disorder.
The proposed disorder–response relationship should hold from approximately 500°C to 1000°C.
The 500°C–1000°C interval corresponds to approximately 0.6–0.8 of the alloy melting temperature.
Outside 500°C–1000°C, phase transformations or other deformation mechanisms may dominate.
Related refractory HEAs exhibit temperature-dependent yield strength and work-hardening/softening behavior at elevated temperatures.
Grain size and residual stress could contribute to the measured mechanical and thermal responses.
The controlled comparison consists of rapidly quenched and annealed HfNbTaTiZr samples tested under the same in-situ thermal and mechanical conditions.
Failure of the higher-disorder samples to show lower modulus and yield strength together with higher thermal expansion over 500°C–1000°C would refute the proposed relationship.
